chunks: Abu Ali Al-Ash'ari, from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Jabbar, from Ahmad ibn al-Nadr, from Abu Ja'far al-Fazari, who said:
Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) called a slave of his named Musadif and gave him one thousand dinars, and said to him: 'Equip yourself until you go out to Egypt, for my dependents have multiplied.'

He said: So he equipped himself with goods and went out with the merchants to Egypt. When they approached Egypt, a caravan coming out of Egypt met them. They asked them about the goods they had, what its condition was in the city, and the goods were general commodities. They informed them that there was nothing of it available in Egypt. So they swore oaths and made a contract that they would not sell their goods for less than a profit of one dinar per dinar.

When they had collected their wealth and returned to the city, Musadif came to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) with him were two bags, in each of which was one thousand dinars. He said: 'May I be your ransom, this is the capital, and this other is profit.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'This profit is large, but what did you do with the goods?' So he narrated to him how they had acted and how they had sworn oaths.

He said: 'Glory be to Allah! You swear oaths against a group of Muslims that you will not sell to them except for a profit of a dinar per dinar.' Then he took one of the bags and said: 'This is my capital, and we have no need for this profit.' Then he said: 'O Musadif! A dispute of swords is easier than seeking the permissible (halal).'

key_terms.تَحَالَفُوا: They swore mutual oaths (to form a pact)
key_terms.مُصَادِفٌ: Musadif (a slave/agent name, meaning one who meets or encounters)

ai.seo_question: What is the lesson on trade ethics and profit margins in this hadith from Imam al-Sadiq?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Al-Kafi* illustrates the principle of *Gharar* (uncertainty) and fair pricing in Shia commercial jurisprudence, where Imam al-Sadiq (AS) critiques the merchants' self-imposed monopoly rather than the profit itself. By rejecting the excessive gain derived from exploiting market scarcity, the Imam emphasizes that securing *Halal* sustenance requires rigorous ethical diligence, a struggle he equates to the physical exertion of jihad. This narrative underscores the Shia scholarly view that commercial transactions must be free from both legal defects and moral exploitation of the community's needs.

en.hubeali: Abu Ali Al Ashary, from Muhammad Bin Abdul Jabbar, from Ahmad Bin Al Nazar, from Abu Ja’far Al Fazary who said,

‘Abu Abdullah called over a slave of his<sup>asws</sup> called Musadif. So he<sup>asws</sup> gave him a thousand Dinars and said to him: ‘Equip yourself until you go out to Egypt, for my<sup>asws</sup> dependents have multiplied’.

He said, ‘So I equipped myself with belongings and went out along with the merchants to Egypt. So when we approached Egypt, a caravan met them outside of Egypt. So they asked them (Egyptians) about the belongings which were with them, what was its state in the city, and the belongings were general (items). So they (Egyptians) informed them that there was nothing from it available in Egypt. So they vowed and agreed upon that they would not draw out their belongings of a Dinar for a profit less than a Dinar (100% mark-up).

So when they grabbed their wealth (profits) and left to go to Al-Medina, Musadif came over to Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> and with him were two bags, in each of the bags being a thousand Dinars. So he said, ‘May I be sacrificed for you<sup>asws</sup>! This is the capital of the wealth, and this is another, a profit’. So he<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘This profit is a lot, but what did you do regarding the goods?’ So he narrated to him<sup>asws</sup> how he had dealt and how they had all oathed (for doubling of the price).

So he<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘Glory be to Allah<sup>azwj</sup>! They were oathing against a group of Muslims that they would not be selling to them except for a profit of a Dinar with the Dinar?’ Then he<sup>asws</sup> took one of the bags, so he<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘This is the capital of my<sup>asws</sup> wealth, and there is no need for us<sup>asws</sup> with regards to this profit’. Then he<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘O Musadif! A dispute of the swords is easier than seeking the Permissible’.
en.sarwar: 1. Abu Ali al-Ash’ariy has narrated from Muhammad ibn ‘Abd al-Jabbar from Ahmad ibn abu Nadr from abu Ja’far al-Fazariy who has said the following:

“Once abu Ja‘far, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, called one of his servants named Musadif and gave him a thousand dinar. He (the Imam) told him to prepare for traveling to Egypt and added, ‘The number of my dependents has increased.’

He (the narrator) has said that the servant prepared certain items of merchandise along with the traders to go for trade to Egypt. When they arrived near Egypt they met a caravan coming out of Egypt. They asked the outgoing caravan with regards to the condition of their merchandise, which was of general nature, in the city. The outgoing people informed them that no such merchandise was available in the city. They (people of the incoming caravan) made an agreement among themselves on oath not to sell their merchandise for less than a profit of one dinar for each dinar worth of merchandise.

After taking possession of their belongings, they returned to al-Madinah and Musadif came to abu ‘Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, with two bagfuls of dinars, each of which had a thousand dinars. He said, ‘I pray to Allah to keep my soul in service for your cause, this is the capital and this is the profit.’ He (the Imam) said, ‘This is a great deal of profit. However, what did you do with the merchandise?’ He (Musadif) told the story of their agreement on oath.

He (the Imam) said, ‘Allah is free of all defects. Why do you make an agreement on oath against a Muslim people not to sell for less than a profit of one dinar for each dinar worth of merchandise?’ He (the Imam) then took the two bags and said, ‘This is my capital and we do not need this profit.’ He (the Imam) said, ‘O Musadif, settling with sword is easier than earning by lawful ways.’”
